metadata.title: Profit Sharing with Equal Investment Periods
metadata.description: Reduce capital contributions to a ratio and allocate a known gain or loss when partners invest for the same duration.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: For equal investment periods, form the profit/loss ratio directly from capital contributions. Reduce monetary amounts without changing their order, allocate a known total by ratio parts, and find a partner’s share or total from one known share. Include capital ratios given as fractions, percentages, multiples, or differences, and check that allocated shares sum to the stated total. Ground in solved examples 1 and 4 and objective patterns 1–8, 27–28, and 33–35.

content.text: Profit Sharing with Equal Investment Periods: Reduce capital contributions to a ratio and allocate a known gain or loss when partners invest for the same duration. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

Profit Sharing with Equal Investment Periods asks you to decide what determines each partner’s share. Reduce capital contributions to a ratio and allocate a known gain or loss when partners invest for the same duration. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. When partners invest for the same length of time, capital alone determines their relative shares. Write the partner names and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

If all durations equal t, then C₁t:C₂t simplifies to C₁:C₂; the common time factor cancels. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once both are expressed in compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: Capitals ₹45,000 and ₹70,000 reduce to 9:14. Out of ₹46,000 profit, one part is ₹2,000, so the second partner gets ₹28,000. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Reduce the capital ratio once, then use total parts to find the amount per part. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. The ratio parts must sum to the total profit, and each calculated share must add back to that total. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: Do not multiply by a duration twice when it is equal for everyone; do not divide by only one partner’s capital. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. Capital ratios can be encoded as fractions, percentages, sums, or differences; translate those conditions before allocation. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for profit sharing with equal investment periods without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
